headline: Coral reefs are the rainforests of the sea—built by tiny animals over thousands of years
universal_truth: Small, consistent actions compound into magnificent structures
fun_facts: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support 25% of all marine species
The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on Earth—visible from space
Corals are animals, not plants—tiny relatives of jellyfish that build limestone skeletons
discussion_questions: What structure are you slowly building through small, consistent actions?
Why do coral reefs support so much more life than the surrounding ocean?
What can the slow building of reefs teach us about patience?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: They look like colorful rocks or underwater forests. But coral reefs are cities—built by billions of tiny animals over thousands of years. Each polyp is smaller than a pencil eraser. Together, they create the largest living structures on Earth.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean but support 25% of all marine species. The surrounding ocean is practically a desert. How do these tiny builders create such islands of abundance?
cliff.prompt: How do coral reefs support so much life?

options.text: They create complex 3D structure with countless niches for different species
options.response: Yes. Structure creates diversity. The reef's complexity offers hiding spots, hunting grounds, and nurseries.

options.text: Warm tropical waters near reefs support more marine life
options.response: Warm water helps, but bare warm water is still empty...

q1.title: Animal Architects
q1.script: Corals are animals—tiny polyps related to jellyfish. Each polyp builds a limestone cup around itself. When it dies, the skeleton remains, and new polyps build on top. Layer by layer, over millennia, reefs rise. The structure you see is mostly skeleton.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Animal Architects"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Symbiotic Power
q2.script: Inside each coral polyp live microscopic algae called zooxanthellae. The algae photosynthesize and share nutrients with the coral. In return, the coral provides shelter. This partnership is so essential that when stressed corals expel their algae—bleaching—they often die.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Visible From Space
q3.script: The Great Barrier Reef stretches 1,400 miles—the largest living structure on Earth, visible from space. It was built by organisms you can barely see. Small actions, repeated over time, created something that astronauts photograph from orbit.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Magnificent structures are built one small action at a time. The coral polyp doesn't see the reef—it just builds its tiny cup, day after day. Your small, consistent actions are building something you may not yet see.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 63. Tomorrow, we'll explore worlds without light. Until then, consider: what reef are you building, one small action at a time?
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Small Builder - Compound Your Actions
growTrack.learning_objective: Recognize how small consistent actions create large results
growTrack.activity: Identify one small action you could do consistently that would compound over time—a daily practice, a weekly connection, a regular contribution. What might 'your reef' look like in 5 years if you kept building?
